pages.text: Investing is when you put money in assets with the intention of them growing in their value, making money when you decide to sell these assets.
There are many different kinds of investments, including stocks, bonds, real estate, raw materials, and collectibles.
We will focus on stocks here.
A stock is part of a company.
This means when you own a stock, you own a part of the company.
If the company's value increases, so does your stock.
By buying percentages of companies that grow over time, so does your investment.
Investing can have many benefits including a voice in the company's decisions and growing your wealth.
When your money isn't invested you actually lose money over time due to inflation.
Currencies around the world often lose value anually due to a process known as inflation.
In the United States, the inflation rate has been close to 2% anually.
What this means is cash saved will decrease in spending power by 2% each year.
For example, if an apple is $1 and someone has $100, 100 apples could be purchased. If the $100 was saved, in 40 years--assuming a 2% inflation rate--only 44 apples could be purchased.

This provides an argument for investing money. If an investment grows by 10% each year--subtracting the 2% value loss from inflation--2,172 apples could be purchased. The next lesson will show what makes this growth rate feasible.
An index fund is a large collection of stocks that can be purchased as one unit.
One of the most well known index funds is the S&P 500 fund.
The S&P 500 is a group of the top 500 companies in the United States.
The S&P 500 index fund has had a historical growth rate of around 10% each year.

Assuming this growth rate--10% from the S&P 500 minus 2% from inflation-- investing $100 each month into the S&P 500 will create $313,040 in 40 years. With the inflation rate of 2%, this investment would be worth $33,330. That's more than a 9x increase in money in one's pocket from supporting the United States economy!
